meta.title: Who really said "The socialism I believe in is everyone working for each other, everyone having a share of the rewards. It's the way I see football, the way I see life"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Bill Shankly wrote it, but longer. His 1976 autobiography adds "everyone helping each other" and "at the end of the day." The famous one-liner is a condensation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The socialism I believe in is everyone working for each other, everyone having a share of the rewards. It's the way I see football, the way I see life'?
meta.ogDescription: Shankly's own book says it at greater length. The tidy one-line version in circulation is a later condensation, not a sentence he wrote.

answer.label: Bill Shankly — but not in these words
answer.sourceLine: Shankly did say this, at greater length: his 1976 autobiography Shankly — an as-told-to book written with the journalist John Roberts — has it in full, and full-text search inside the scanned book confirms the passage “…by collective effort, with everyone working for each other, everyone helping each other, and everyone having a share of the rewards at the end of the day. That might be asking a lot, but it’s the way I see football and the way I see life.” The tidy one-line version in circulation is a later condensation — it drops “everyone helping each other,” drops “at the end of the day,” and drops the qualifier “that might be asking a lot” — and that exact sentence appears nowhere in his own book.

source.excerpt: The socialism I believe in is not really politics. It is a way of living. It is humanity. I believe the only way to live and to be truly successful is by collective effort, with everyone working for each other, everyone helping each other, and everyone having a share of the rewards at the end of the day. That might be asking a lot, but it’s the way I see football and the way I see life.
trail: Shankly’s own autobiography carries the long form. A full-text search for “That might be asking a lot, but it’s the way I see football” ↗ returns Shankly by Bill Shankly, with the snippet continuing “and the way I see life.”

The short one-liner is not in that book. A search for the popular wording ↗ returns about a dozen results, all later books — Dave Zirin’s Bad Sports, Gabriel Kuhn’s Soccer vs. the State, Nick Davidson’s Modern Football Is Still Rubbish and others — but not Shankly’s own.

Wikiquote ↗ lists the short wording in its main quotes section, sourcing it not to Shankly but to Adam Powley and Robert Gillan’s Shankly’s Village (Pitch, 2015) — a book published nearly four decades after the autobiography.
Open Library’s record for the work ↗ confirms Shankly was first published in 1976 by Barker, with a Readers Union printing the following year — the copy that was scanned.
source.excerptNote: Confirmed by full-text search inside the scanned book ↗, which returns Shankly by Bill Shankly among the matches. The scan’s OCR renders the first full stop as a comma (“not really politics, It is a way of living”); the punctuation above follows the reading printed in the many later books that reproduce the passage.

author.name: Bill Shankly
author.kicker: The man who said it — at greater length
author.heading: Bill Shankly
author.metaLine: 1913–1981 · Liverpool manager 1959–1974 · Glenbuck miner turned football’s great evangelist
author.bio: Born in Glenbuck, an Ayrshire coal village, Shankly worked in the pit after leaving school in 1928 before playing for Carlisle United and then Preston North End. He managed Carlisle, Grimsby, Workington and Huddersfield before taking over a Second Division Liverpool in 1959 and leaving, fifteen years later, with three league titles, two FA Cups and a UEFA Cup. His 1976 autobiography, Shankly, is where the socialism passage appears — written not as a manifesto but as a description of how he thought a dressing room, and a life, ought to work.

That might be asking a lot, but it's the way I see football and the way I see life.” The shorter one-sentence version in wide circulation does not appear in the book.

misattribution.heading: The wording keeps shrinking
misattribution.intro: Nobody is stealing this line from Shankly. What has happened instead is attrition: each retelling files off another clause until a paragraph becomes a slogan. At least three different “exact quotes” are now in circulation, and none of them is the sentence he wrote.

items.who: “everyone working for each other, everyone having a share of the rewards. It’s the way I see football, the way I see life”
items.why: The version on this page. It appears in later books — Zirin, Kuhn, Davidson, Rostron and others ↗ — but a search inside Shankly’s own book does not return it. Three clauses have been cut: “everyone helping each other,” “at the end of the day,” and the hedge “that might be asking a lot.”

items.who: “everybody working for the same goal and everybody having a share in the rewards. That’s how I see football, that’s how I see life”
items.why: A further rewrite that swaps “for each other” for “for the same goal.” Wikiquote parked it on its talk page under “Unsourced” ↗ rather than in the article, precisely because nobody could point to where he said it.

items.who: “everyone working together, everyone having a share of the rewards… It’s the way I see football, the way I see life”
items.why: A third form, with “working together” in place of “working for each other,” which turns up in The Pocket Book of Liverpool ↗ introduced with the vague tag “he once said.”

misattribution.truthLine: What the autobiography actually records, and what the scan of his own book confirms ↗, is longer and less certain of itself: socialism as “not really politics … a way of living … humanity,” achieved by collective effort — and then, disarmingly, “that might be asking a lot.”

context.heading: Why the missing clause matters
lead: Shankly grew up in Glenbuck, an Ayrshire pit village, and went down the mine with his brother Bob after leaving school in 1928 ↗, until the pit closed and he faced unemployment. When he wrote about socialism decades later, he was not reaching for a political programme; he was describing the only economics he had ever seen work — a shift where everyone pulls or nobody eats.

The condensation is a better slogan and a worse portrait. Shankly’s own paragraph contains a clause the one-liner always cuts: that might be asking a lot. He knew he was describing an ideal, not a settled fact about football or about Britain. Strip the hedge and you turn a man who hoped into a man who pronounced.
detailsBody: The book itself was late work. Shankly announced his retirement as Liverpool manager on 12 July 1974, after fifteen years in the job, and the autobiography followed in 1976. He died in 1981.

The passage travels far outside football writing: the same lines are quoted in academic and political books, from Stephen G. Jones’s Sport, Politics, and the Working Class to Simon Critchley’s What We Think About When We Think About Football — which is exactly the sort of circulation that sands a paragraph down into a sentence.
context.pull: “That might be asking a lot” — the four words the famous version always deletes.

Open Library full-text search for "It is a way of living. It is humanity" returns "Shankly." by Bill Shankly among the matching books, with the snippet "believe in is not really politics, It is a way of living. It is humanity. I believe the only way to live..."
Open Library full-text search for "That might be asking a lot, but it's the way I see football" returns "Shankly." by Bill Shankly, with the snippet continuing "and the way I see life".

Open Library full-text search for the popular short wording "everyone working for each other, everyone having a share of the rewards" returns about a dozen results across roughly nine distinct later titles (Bad Sports and Soccer vs. the State each returned twice) — including Dave Zirin's Bad Sports, Gabriel Kuhn's Soccer vs. the State, Nick Davidson's Modern Football Is Still Rubbish and Phil Rostron's We are the Damned United — and does NOT return Shankly's own autobiography.

Open Library full-text search for "everyone having a share of the rewards" returns The Pocket Book of Liverpool with the variant snippet "everyone working together, everyone having a share of the rewards," he once said. "It's the way I..." — and returns "Shankly." by Bill Shankly with the different snippet "everyone helping each other, and everyone having a share of the rewards at the end of the day."
Open Library's work record confirms Shankly, by Bill Shankly, was first published in 1976, with editions from Barker (1976, ISBN 9780213166038) and Readers Union (1977).
The Internet Archive holds a scanned copy of Shankly's autobiography: "Shankly." by Bill Shankly, Readers Union, 1977, 214 pages.

The autobiography was an as-told-to book produced with the journalist John Roberts: the modern reissue, "Shankly: My Story" (Trinity Mirror Sport Media, 2009), is catalogued with John Roberts credited as an author alongside Bill Shankly.

Wikipedia records that Bill Shankly was born 2 September 1913 in Glenbuck, Ayrshire, died 29 September 1981, worked at the local mine with his brother Bob after leaving school in 1928 until the pit closed, played for Carlisle United and Preston North End, managed Carlisle, Grimsby Town, Workington, Huddersfield Town and then Liverpool from 1959 to 1974, winning three First Division titles, two FA Cups and the UEFA Cup, and announced his retirement on 12 July 1974.
